assessment.nobel_worthiness: Fluctuation theorems (Evans-Searles, Jarzynski equality, Crooks relation) are exact, general statements that extend the second law to small, driven, far-from-equilibrium systems and relate nonequilibrium work to equilibrium free energies. This is the kind of simple, universal and rigorously provable mechanism I value, and it spans single-molecule biophysics, colloids, nanoscale thermodynamics and quantum devices. Its importance is conceptual and it is understood, not just useful.
assessment.attribution: Jarzynski (work relation, 1997) and Crooks (detailed fluctuation relation, 1999) are clear. Evans and collaborators (Evans-Cohen-Morriss, Evans-Searles) gave the earlier steady-state fluctuation theorem. The supplied credit omits Gallavotti and Cohen, whose chaotic-hypothesis route is a real competing claim, and Kurchan, Lebowitz-Spohn and Hatano-Sasa also matter, so a clean three-person split is contestable.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally confirmed repeatedly since about 2002 (RNA hairpin pulling by Bustamante and colleagues, optical traps, nanoscale and quantum systems), with stable interpretation and about 25 years of maturity. Recognition would be timely.
uncertainties: Whether the committee can justify omitting Gallavotti and Cohen, and whether the Bustamante-style experiments deserve credit.
Some of the field's impact is conceptual rather than technological, which may weigh against it in a prize framed by discovery or invention.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Liquid-liquid phase separation as an organising principle of the cell (P granules, nucleoli, stress granules) brings soft-matter and statistical physics directly into biology. The core idea is a simple mechanism, phase separation of multivalent macromolecules, that explains compartmentalisation without membranes. It is a rare case of physics ideas reshaping cell biology.
assessment.attribution: Brangwynne, Hyman and colleagues showed liquid-like P granules in 2009, and Jülicher supplied the physical theory of active droplets and condensate dynamics. A fair physics-prize triple is plausible, but the field is large and broad (Rosen, Fawzi, Pappu, Banani, Taylor and others), and the biology may be judged a Chemistry or Medicine matter.
assessment.maturity: Strongly replicated across many labs in about 15 years, but the physiological relevance of phase separation versus other assemblies is still debated, and in vivo material properties and disease links are still being worked out. Probably slightly early for a physics prize.
uncertainties: Debate over which cellular structures are truly liquid-like and functionally dependent on phase separation.
Prize-category fit: physics versus chemistry or physiology/medicine.
Large community and diffuse credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect revealed a new class of quantum matter with robust edge states protected by time-reversal symmetry, building on the 2016 topological-phase prize. The theory (Z2 invariant) and observation in HgTe quantum wells are clean and very influential across condensed matter, materials science and cold atoms.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele gave the Z2 classification and the quantum spin Hall prediction in graphene (2005). Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted it in HgTe, and Molenkamp's group observed it in 2007. Hasan's three-dimensional work and Fu, Kane and Mele's 3D theory also have claims. Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is a coherent theory-plus-experiment triple, but the omission of Zhang (deceased) and Bernevig complicates it.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many independent groups, including Bi2Se3-class materials, and now textbook knowledge. Timing is mature. The 2016 prize partly overlaps in subject, which is a consideration.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2016 Nobel for topological phase transitions and phases.
Allocation among Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan, Bernevig and Zhang; Zhang's death limits his eligibility.
Whether the quantum anomalous Hall experimental line should be a separate recognition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory is an exactly controlled limit (infinite dimensions) that turns strongly correlated lattice problems into self-consistent quantum impurity problems. It gave the first reliable account of the Mott transition and, combined with ab initio methods, is the standard tool for correlated materials. It is an elegant mechanism-level theory with a clear conceptual origin.
assessment.attribution: Metzner and Vollhardt (1989) introduced the infinite-dimensional limit, Müller-Hartmann also contributed, and Georges and Kotliar (1992) made the mapping to an impurity problem, with Jarrell too. The credited three-person set is reasonable but the omission of Metzner and Jarrell is a real concern. Georges-Kotliar-Vollhardt is plausible.
assessment.maturity: More than 30 years old with extensive validation against experiments and numerics, and widespread use in LDA+DMFT. Recognition is arguably overdue and stable.
uncertainties: Credit for the original limit (Metzner, Müller-Hartmann) and for the impurity-solver step (Jarrell) is not in the supplied names.
Quantitative predictive accuracy for specific materials remains method-dependent.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene gave a tunable platform for flat-band correlated insulators and superconductivity, launching the moire materials field. The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model gives a simple prediction of the magic angle, which fits my taste for a simple model that unexpectedly explains a messy system, and the experiments of 2018 confirmed it.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald (2011) predicted flat bands near 1.1 degrees, and Jarillo-Herrero's group (Cao et al., 2018) found correlated insulators and superconductivity. Other claims exist (Dean, Kim and Yacoby on moire transport, Kim, Ashoori, Efetov, and early theory by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, and Suarez Morell), which complicates a three-person prize.
assessment.maturity: Strongly replicated and rapidly extended (fractional Chern insulators, nematicity, STM), but the superconducting mechanism and the nature of correlated states remain unsettled, so the field is still developing.
uncertainties: Unresolved mechanism for superconductivity and correlated states.
Credit for earlier theory (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) and experimental competitors.
Might be premature compared with older, settled candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and enable tests of fundamental physics, relativistic geodesy and a possible redefinition of the second. This is a major precision-measurement advance with clear lasting impact.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice (2001-2003) and demonstrated the first strontium lattice clock. Ye's group pushed accuracy and stability, including many-body (spin-polarised fermion) clocks. A two-person split is natural, though comb work (Hall and Hänsch, already recognised in 2005) and ion-clock competitors (Wineland, 2012) are neighbours, and others (Lemonde, Derevianko, Bloom) contributed.
assessment.maturity: Mature and independently reproduced by several international laboratories, with the redefinition of the second pending. Recognition is timely, though a close relation to the 2005 and 2012 prizes could dampen novelty.
uncertainties: Overlap with previous frequency-metrology prizes.
Contributions of Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom and others are not in the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation of lattice models with ultracold atoms realises Hubbard-type Hamiltonians in controllable form, from the superfluid-Mott transition to quantum gas microscopes. For a theorist of many-body systems it makes statistical-mechanics models experimentally accessible, and it is broad and conceptually important.
assessment.attribution: Jaksch, Zoller and colleagues proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation in 1998. Greiner, Hänsch and Bloch observed the Mott transition in 2002, and Bloch led much of the later development, including gas microscopes (Greiner, Bakr, Gross). Jaksch is missing, Cirac is also credited, and the overlap with Ketterle and Zoller's other candidates makes allocation uncertain.
assessment.maturity: Extensively confirmed and now a large research field, but its 'discovery' character is distributed, and the major impact so far is methodological rather than a single result. The 2001 BEC prize and 2012 prize are neighbouring recognitions.
uncertainties: Credit for the theoretical proposal (Jaksch, Zoller) versus experiments and microscopy.
Overlap with candidates in trapped-ion and Rydberg-array quantum simulation, which share Zoller and Cirac.
Whether a broad 'quantum simulation' field fits a prize for a specific discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Direct observation of Anderson localization of matter waves in disordered optical potentials confirms a foundational concept in disordered quantum systems and random matrices in a clean, controllable setting. It makes the physics of localization explicit, which is conceptually close to my own work on random-matrix theory and disordered systems.
assessment.attribution: The 2008 results came from two groups, Aspect and colleagues (Billy et al., Orsay/Palaiseau) and Inguscio's group in Florence (Roati et al., with Modugno). Anderson himself was recognised in 1977, and Aspect holds a 2022 prize, which makes a prize configuration less attractive. Chabe, Jendrzejewski, Sanchez-Palencia and Bouyer are among others who contributed, and the supplied three-name set is plausible but not complete.
assessment.maturity: Replicated in one, two and three dimensions, including the 3D mobility edge, so the confirmation is strong, but the discovery is an implementation of an established theory and the wider impact is narrower than other candidates.
uncertainties: Novelty: experimental realisation of a theoretical prediction already honoured in 1977.
Aspect already received the 2022 prize, and three-dimensional results had competing groups and interpretations (Hulet, DeMarco, Delande).
Whether the community regards this as a prize-level discovery.
